channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: MIA Watchlist: Track 15 July China Q2 GDP and the India-UK FTA launch, whether the Hormuz 20% toll is actually enforced, the stalled EU Industrial Accelerator Act, the next US CPI print, and Europe's sub-one-month jet-fuel cover.
item.description:
• 15 July double event: China releases Q2 GDP (~4.3-4.6%) and the India-UK FTA enters force — confirming the slowing-China and bloc-building threads.
  • Hormuz enforcement: Watch whether the US 20% toll is administered and how Gulf allies react; enforceability, not the announcement, sets the oil and freight path.
  • EU Industrial Accelerator Act: A year-end sign-off is now in doubt — slippage would confirm the deindustrialisation risk case.
  • US CPI print: The report Waller flagged as decisive for the rate path; an energy-driven upside surprise hardens the hawkish tilt.
  • European distillate stocks: Sub-one-month jet-fuel cover is the tightest supply metric of the conflict; a further draw shifts the shock from price to availability.

item.title: Indonesia is preparing an EPR rule requiring ~10,000 makers of plastic-packaged goods to fund waste management, while the EAEU opened an anti-dumping probe into Chinese multi-layer packaging — regulation moving packaging costs in two regions at once.
item.description:
Both actions reprice packaging inputs. Indonesia's EPR shifts collection and recycling costs onto producers via packaging-recovery organisations, part of a global EPR wave. The EAEU probe — triggered by Russian firms after Chinese multi-layer-packaging imports rose 15% against a 2% demand fall — signals protectionism reaching packaging materials. Together with the EU tyre duties (see other insight in this alert), they show trade and environmental regulation converging on materials-intensive segments.

Industry Impact

Packaging is a significant adhesives and coatings end-market. EPR schemes raise the pull for recyclable and mono-material designs, favouring adhesive and barrier-coating chemistries compatible with recycling — a product-development signal, not just a cost. The EAEU anti-dumping probe may open regional substitution opportunities but also fragments the packaging-materials market along trade-bloc lines. Track EPR expansion across ASEAN as a design-requirement driver for packaging adhesives.

Jakarta Post | Bumprom.ru

item.title: Bank of Baroda raised India's FY27 growth to 6.6-6.8%, Vietnam's cumulative FDI hit USD 550bn with H1 commitments up 61%, and Taiwan's Academia Sinica lifted 2026 growth to 10.16% on AI — Asian economies compounding while the West tightens.
item.description:
The contrast with the developed-market picture (slowing US, weak Germany, cooling China headline) is the point. India's upgrade rests on domestic resilience and cheaper fuel; Vietnam's FDI surge reflects supply-chain diversification away from China; Taiwan's near-double-digit forecast is almost entirely AI-driven, tying its fortunes to the same capex cycle now wobbling in equity markets (see other insight in this alert). These are the growth pools absorbing global manufacturing reallocation.

Industry Impact

India and Vietnam are the clearest medium-term demand-growth and manufacturing-footprint opportunities for ACS producers, as global manufacturers diversify sourcing there. Taiwan's AI-linked expansion supports high-value electronics adhesives but carries capex-cycle risk. The strategic read: weight incremental capacity and commercial investment toward these Asian growth pools rather than saturated, contracting Western end-markets.

Business Standard | Kompas | Commercial Times (Taiwan) | The Hindu Business Line

item.title: Fed Governor Waller warned the central bank may need to hike near-term if inflation stays well above 2%, citing possible energy-cost surges; a WSJ survey lifted 2026 US growth to 2.1% and cut recession odds to 25%, but raised expected CPI to 3.4%.
item.description:
The hawkish shift ties directly to the Hormuz shock (see other insight in this alert): Waller names energy costs and broadening price pressures as the risks that could delay reaching 2%. The improving growth-and-lower-recession picture is being offset by firmer inflation — a classic late-cycle squeeze. US manufacturing employment underlines the fragility: June added just 3,000 jobs but remained ~38,000 below a year earlier and ~75,000 below January 2025, with investment declining.

Industry Impact

A Fed leaning toward hikes pressures the rate-sensitive end-markets ACS depends on — US housing (already showing strain) and autos. Combined with oil-driven feedstock inflation, this is margin-negative on both sides of the P&L. US-exposed coatings and adhesives demand should be planned conservatively for H2; any Hormuz-driven energy spike would reinforce the hawkish path and deepen the demand drag.

The Economic Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Los Angeles Times

item.title: Germany funded 50,000 attack drones for Ukraine (~USD 103m, the largest Western order yet) and France for the first time licensed Ukraine to make French missiles, yet Macron called go-it-alone national defence an "absurdity" after FCAS collapsed.
item.description:
The build-up and the fragmentation are the same story. Germany's Shrike FPV order (SkyFall drones, US Auterion autonomy software) and France's licensing breakthrough show rapid capacity expansion, while the Coalition of the Willing coordinates pressure on Moscow. But Macron's warning — a month after the Franco-German FCAS collapse over industrial rivalries — exposes the structural weakness: Europe is spending more without a unified industrial base, the same fault line the deindustrialisation paper identifies (see other insight in this alert).

Industry Impact

Defence is a rising demand pillar for specialty ACS: structural adhesives, protective and stealth coatings, and sealants for drones, missiles and aircraft. Accelerating European procurement is a multi-year tailwind for defence-grade chemical inputs. The fragmentation caveat matters commercially — a splintered European defence-industrial base means multiple national supply chains rather than one scale programme, favouring suppliers who can serve several national primes rather than betting on a single flagship platform.

Chinatimes | Lianhe Zaobao | The Guardian | The Straits Times (missiles) | The Straits Times (Macron)

item.title: Berlin plans tax cuts worth partly over EUR 600/year per household, even as the ifo residential-construction climate fell to -31.0 in June and firms citing order shortages rose to 43.7% — stimulus meeting a sector still contracting.
item.description:
The two signals sit in tension. The fiscal-relief package targets consumption, but the construction data show infrastructure debt and the "construction turbo" have not stabilised sentiment; material-supply worries persist and the Hormuz closure is explicitly cited as a new drag. The delta from prior runs is a hardening of the German split: fiscal ambition on one side, real-economy weakness in the most chemical-intensive downstream sector on the other. Eurozone composite PMI has edged back toward the boom-bust line, but German external demand remains the weak link.

Industry Impact

Residential construction is a primary end-market for sealants, adhesives and architectural coatings; a -31 climate reading signals continued volume pressure in Germany, the ACS industry's core European market. The tax package may support renovation demand at the margin but will not offset a structural building downturn. Plan for soft German construction-chemicals volumes through H2, with any upside dependent on infrastructure disbursement actually reaching sites.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Tagesschau | Commercial Times (PMI)

item.title: A Reuters poll expects China's Q2 GDP at 4.5% (down from 5.0%), with full-year 2026 cooling to 4.6%, yet NEV exports jumped 120% in H1 and investment in AI and humanoid robots rose 118% — a slowing headline masking an accelerating industrial upgrade.
item.description:
The 15 July release will confirm weak domestic demand — April consumption grew just 0.2% — driving stimulus expectations. But the composition is the story: China is trading broad growth for concentrated advance in exportable high-tech manufacturing. NEV exports up 120%, robot exports near CNY 20bn in five months, and Japanese carmakers' China sales collapsing (Honda -44.5% in June) show domestic share shifting to local champions while export muscle builds. This is the mechanism behind the European deindustrialisation warning (see other insight in this alert).

Industry Impact

A slower but upgrading China is double-edged for ACS producers: weaker construction and consumption dampen commodity-coatings demand, while the NEV and robotics surge lifts high-value automotive and electronics adhesives — but increasingly served by Chinese domestic suppliers. The competitive threat is that China's export machine now includes the specialty inputs Western chemical firms sell. Watch the 15 July print and any stimulus skewed to property, which would directly move construction-chemicals demand.

MarketScreener | Commercial Times | China Economic Net | Global Times | Commercial Times (Japan brands)

item.title: A Centre for European Reform paper warns Europe faces deindustrialisation at China's hand: the EU's goods deficit with China is roughly Italy's GDP and growing ~30% a year, while the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act slips behind schedule.
item.description:
This is the structural frame behind the reshoring data (see other insight in this alert) and the VW crisis it was written around. The Industrial Accelerator Act — meant to release billions in subsidies and public procurement — may not be signed off by year-end, leaving Europe without its main policy counterweight just as the deficit accelerates. It converges with the German raw-materials debate over circular-economy dependence and supply-chain resilience findings showing trade resilience deteriorating across 157 countries.

Industry Impact

Deindustrialisation is an existential-tail risk for European ACS demand: adhesives, coatings and sealants are mid-chain inputs that shrink with the manufacturing base they serve, and a stalled IAA removes a potential demand tailwind. The strategic read for a European-headquartered chemical producer is to hedge geographically — grow exposure to reshoring winners (autos, defence, select construction) while not over-indexing to a European industrial base under structural pressure.

The Guardian | Frankfurter Rundschau | CIPS

item.title: A T&E study shows the "Made in China" share of Western carmakers' EVs sold in Europe fell from 38% to 23% after EU tariffs, while definitive anti-dumping duties of up to 45.3% on Chinese tyres took effect 8 July — tariffs are relocating industry.
item.description:
The reshoring is real but partial: BMW, Volvo, Smart, Dacia and Tesla shifted output back to Europe, yet Chinese brands BYD and Geely kept expanding imports on the back of domestic overproduction. The tyre duties (4.3%-45.3%, Zodo Group at 24.4%) extend the same logic from vehicles to components. This is the constructive counterpart to the deindustrialisation warning (see other insight in this alert): tariffs can pull production back, but only where Western capacity and cost structures allow.

Industry Impact

Reshored EV and tyre production in Europe is a direct positive for European ACS suppliers — automotive adhesives, coatings and sealants demand follows the assembly line, and the tyre duties specifically favour EU-based rubber-chemical and adhesive supply. The caveat is cost: relocation raises input prices, and if European producers cannot match Chinese cost curves the volume gain erodes. Position for a near-term demand uplift in automotive-linked ACS in Europe, with margin discipline.

Handelsblatt | Wallstreet:online | Yahoo Germany

item.title: Three Western-facing trade deals advanced in a day — the India-UK FTA enters force 15 July, the UK-Switzerland deal was concluded, and the India-US framework is ready to sign — a bloc-building response to US tariff weaponisation.
item.description:
The India-UK FTA removes tariffs on 99% of Indian exports and cuts duties on 90% of UK goods, benefiting UK vehicles and spirits and Indian textiles and leather; New Delhi treats it as a template for wider Western deals. The UK-Switzerland pact adds ~CHF 7.9bn/year (25%) in bilateral trade with visa-free services access — the UK's sixth deal in two years. India-US remains framework-only, with New Delhi seeking a tariff edge over competitors. Together they mark a pivot to bilateral bloc-building as the multilateral order fragments.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers the signal is a re-mapping of tariff geography: supply chains routed through India, the UK and Switzerland gain preferential access, while the absence of a signed India-US deal keeps that corridor uncertain. Coatings and adhesives feedstocks and finished goods moving along these lanes should be re-evaluated for tariff arbitrage. The broader lesson is that market access is now negotiated bilaterally and shifts quickly — sourcing footprints need the flexibility to follow.

South China Morning Post | Handelsblatt | Financial Times | Business Standard

item.title: The EU sanctioned 13 entities and individuals including GRU officers, and the UK 24, over a Russian espionage and infrastructure-sabotage network active since 2010; Germany summoned Russia's ambassador — a coordinated hardening rather than a new rupture.
item.description:
The action names GRU-linked officers, hacktivist fronts and private companies accused of targeting government systems and critical infrastructure — heating and power plants — across at least nine countries. The coordination between Brussels and London, timed alongside Macron's Coalition of the Willing (see other insight in this alert), signals a synchronised European posture. It extends, rather than breaks, the sanctions trajectory, but the explicit focus on physical-infrastructure sabotage raises the operational-risk baseline for industrial sites.

Industry Impact

The named targeting of power and heating infrastructure is the relevant signal for chemical producers: sites are energy-intensive and increasingly digitised, and a documented sabotage campaign against exactly this infrastructure strengthens the case for OT-security and energy-resilience investment. The regulatory direction — including the EU Cyber Resilience Act pressure on industrial supply chains — points to rising compliance costs across connected manufacturing.

AP | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Le Figaro | The Straits Times

item.title: European jet-fuel stockpiles cover less than one month of demand, with Britain, France and Germany most exposed and a potential ~600,000-barrel deficit during peak summer travel, as Hormuz disruption threatens the refined-product routes Europe depends on.
item.description:
This is the concrete supply-side consequence the previous alert flagged as a watch item. Europe's exposure is structural: it relies on jet-fuel and middle-distillate shipments transiting Hormuz, and higher imports plus increased refinery runs have not closed the gap. The sub-one-month cover is the tightest signal yet that the conflict is moving from price to availability — a refined-product squeeze, rather than a crude-price spike, is the more damaging channel for European industry.

Industry Impact

Middle-distillate tightness raises freight and energy costs across European manufacturing, directly inflating logistics and drying/curing energy for coatings and adhesives production. A jet-fuel deficit also cascades into aerospace-coatings demand if flight schedules thin. Procurement should stress-test not only crude exposure but refined-product and solvent availability, since naphtha and aromatic solvent chains share the same Hormuz-routed dependency.

Daily Times

item.title: Brent rose 3.9-5% to near USD 79 and the dollar strengthened, while gold fell over 1% and AI/chip equities sold off hard — SK Hynix dropped 15% — signalling the Hormuz shock is being read as inflationary and growth-negative, not a flight to safety.
item.description:
Unlike the previous run, where markets shrugged off the re-closure, the blockade declaration produced a broader repricing. Oil's near-5% intraday spike pared back as traders questioned enforceability, but the direction held. The counterintuitive gold decline reflects dollar strength and rate-hike expectations rather than calm. Most striking is the AI-equity sell-off: SK Hynix -15% in Seoul, with Micron, Intel, Marvell and ARM under pressure, as investors question whether 2026's AI-capex-driven rally can absorb an energy shock.

Industry Impact

A firmer dollar plus higher oil is the worst mix for European ACS producers: input costs rise while export competitiveness holds only if the euro weakens in step. Coatings demand tracks construction and autos, both rate-sensitive — a Fed forced to hold or hike (see other insight in this alert) compounds the demand risk. The AI-equity wobble matters because AI-capex has been the strongest industrial-demand pillar of 2026; if it cools, so does one of the few bright spots for specialty chemicals into electronics.

Cnyes | MarketScreener | Lianhe Zaobao | Finance News Network

item.title: The US moved from retaliatory strikes to a declared naval blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz, charging a 20% toll on all cargo — a qualitative escalation of a conflict that until now stayed below the shipping-disruption line.
item.description:
The delta since the last alert is decisive: a re-closed strait and a third round of strikes have become an open-ended US blockade paired with a fourth airstrike wave, triggered after the Revolutionary Guard hit a container ship. Iran retaliated against US bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman and Jordan and insists ships use its northern territorial channel. Trump framed Washington as "guardian of the strait," keeping it open to all but Iran while levying a 20% charge — an unprecedented monetisation of a chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of global oil and LNG previously moved. The White House gave no detail on administration or allied coordination, which is itself the near-term risk.

Industry Impact

For the chemical and ACS industry the transmission runs through energy and freight, not direct exposure. A sustained toll or interdiction raises crude, naphtha and shipping-insurance costs, lifting feedstock and logistics bills for adhesives, coatings and sealants producers with thin buffers. The bigger risk is a step-change in Gulf-routed petrochemical and base-oil flows; procurement should treat the 20% toll as a de-facto tariff on any Hormuz-routed input and re-price accordingly.

BBC News | The Globe and Mail | The Hindu Business Line | Commercial Times

item.title: MIA Digest: The US declared a formal naval blockade of Iran in the Strait of Hormuz with a 20% cargo toll; oil jumped and AI equities sold off, EU/UK sanctioned Russian intelligence, and a cluster of Western trade deals advanced.
item.description:
• Hormuz blockade, not just strikes: The US declared a formal naval blockade of Iran and a 20% toll on all Hormuz cargo after a fourth airstrike wave — a step-change from last week's re-closure.
  • Markets split on the shock: Brent rose ~4-5% and the dollar firmed while gold and AI chip stocks fell (SK Hynix -15%), reading the escalation as inflationary, not a safe-haven event.
  • Europe's fuel buffer is thin: European jet-fuel stocks cover under one month of demand, with Britain, France and Germany most exposed to a Hormuz refined-product squeeze.
  • Trade blocs rewire around US tariffs: India-UK FTA goes live 15 July, UK-Switzerland concluded, and the India-US framework is ready to sign — bilateral deal-making replaces the multilateral order.
  • Tariffs are relocating industry: Western EV output is returning to Europe (China-made share down 38% to 23%) and new EU tyre duties hit 45.3%, but a CER paper warns of deindustrialisation as the China goods deficit grows ~30%/year.
